entities.name: Epigenes of Byzantium
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Epigenes of Byzantium, an influential Greek astrologer active around 100 BCE, played a pivotal role in the transmission and legitimization of Babylonian astrological knowledge into the Hellenistic world. Operating in the wake of Alexander the Great's conquests, which opened Greek intellectual thought to Mesopotamian traditions, Epigenes served as a crucial conduit, bridging the sophisticated celestial observations of the Chaldeans with the analytical frameworks of Greek philosophy. His work was instrumental in embedding astrology, initially met with skepticism by many Greek intellectuals, as a serious, albeit controversial, discipline within Greco-Roman intellectual discourse.

Epigenes' primary contribution involved the study and dissemination of ancient Babylonian astrological records. He famously referred to vast datasets of observations, including ephemerides and horoscopes, preserved in the temple of Bel in Babylon, claiming they spanned an incredible 720,000 years. While this figure is almost certainly a hyperbolic representation of the perceived antiquity and continuous nature of Mesopotamian astronomical practice, it underscores his engagement with these precise, long-term records. By interpreting and likely translating these Chaldean observations, Epigenes provided a perceived empirical foundation for astrological predictions, thereby enhancing its credibility among his contemporaries and future generations.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Epigenes of Byzantium was a key figure in the transmission of Babylonian astrological knowledge to the Hellenistic world, influencing the development of Greco-Roman astrology and shaping intellectual discourse for centuries, as evidenced by his mention in works like Pliny the Elder's *Natural History*.
